{{Short description|Viceroy of a Canadian province}}
{{Use Canadian English|date=April 2026}}
{{Monarchy of Canada sidebar|viceroys}}
{{Canada provinces map|border=none|align=right|prefix =Lieutenant Governor of|NT=Commissioner of the Northwest Territories|YT=Commissioner of Yukon|NU=Commissioner of Nunavut|caption=Lieutenant governors by province and commissioners by territory}}

In [[Canada]], a '''lieutenant governor''' ({{IPAc-en|l|ɛ|f|ˈ|t|ɛ|n|ə|n|t}}; [[French language|French]] [masculine]: {{lang|fr|lieutenant-gouverneur}}, or [feminine]: {{lang|fr|lieutenante-gouverneure}}) is the representative of the [[King of Canada]] in the government of each [[Canadian provinces and territories|province]]. The [[governor general of Canada]] appoints the lieutenant governors on the [[constitutional advice|advice]] of the [[prime minister of Canada]] to carry out most of the monarch's constitutional and ceremonial duties for an unfixed period of time<ref>{{Cite web |last=Victoria |author-link=Queen Victoria |date=29 March 1867 |title=Constitution Act, 1867 |series=V.58 |url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/ca_1867.html |access-date=15 January 2009 |website=The Solon Law Archive }}</ref>—known as serving "[[At His Majesty's pleasure|at Her Excellency's pleasure]]" — though service for five years is the normal convention. Similar positions in [[Provinces and territories of Canada|Canada's three territories]] are termed "[[Commissioner#Canadian territories|commissioners]]" and are representatives of the federal government, not the monarch directly.

The offices have their roots in the 16th and 17th century colonial governors of [[New France]] and [[British North America]], though the present incarnations of the positions emerged with [[Canadian Confederation]] and the ''[[Constitution Act, 1867|British North America Act]]'' in 1867, which defined the viceregal offices as the "Lieutenant Governor of the Province acting by and with the Advice the [[Executive Council (Canada)|Executive Council]] thereof."<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V.66}}</ref> The posts still ultimately represented the [[government of Canada]] (that is, the [[{{Canadian monarch, current|title=*}}-in-Council|Governor-General-in-Council]]) until the ruling in 1882 of [[William Watson, Baron Watson|the Lord Watson]] of the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council]] in the case of ''[[Maritime Bank v. Receiver-General of New Brunswick]]'',<ref name="Saywell 1957 13–14">{{cite book| last=Saywell| first=John T.| author-link = John Saywell| title=The Office of Lieutenant Governor: A Study in Canadian Government and Politics| url=https://archive.org/details/officeoflieutena0000sayw| url-access=registration| publisher=[[University of Toronto Press]]| year=1957| location=Toronto| pages=[https://archive.org/details/officeoflieutena0000sayw/page/13 13–14]| isbn=9780802070418}}</ref> whereafter the lieutenant governors were recognized as the direct representatives of the monarch.<ref name=Kenney>{{cite web |first=Jason |last=Kenney |author-link=Jason Kenney |title=Speeches – 2007: The Honourable Jason Kenney: Lieutenant Governors Meeting Regina, Saskatchewan |website=Canadian Heritage |date=23 April 2007 |url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pc-ch/minstr/arc_disc-spch/kenney/2007/20070423-eng.cfm |access-date=14 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611163321/http://www.pch.gc.ca/pc-ch/minstr/arc_disc-spch/kenney/2007/20070423-eng.cfm |archive-date=11 June 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book| last=Smith| first=David E.| title=The Invisible Crown| url=https://archive.org/details/invisiblecrownfi0000smit| url-access=registration| publisher=University of Toronto Press| year=1995| location=Toronto| page=[https://archive.org/details/invisiblecrownfi0000smit/page/8 8]| isbn=0-8020-7793-5| ref=CITEREF_Smith_1995}}</ref><ref name="Watson 1892 6">{{Cite book|last=Watson |first=William |author-link=William Watson, Baron Watson |year=1892 |publication-date=2003 |chapter=''Maritime Bank v. Receiver-General of New Brunswick'' |editor-last=Jackson |editor-first=Michael |title=Golden Jubilee and Provincial Crown |periodical=Canadian Monarchist News |volume=7 |issue=3 |page=6 |place=London |publication-place=Toronto |publisher=[[Monarchist League of Canada]] |url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2003/CMN_winter_spring_2003_Update-3.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708032502/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2003/CMN_winter_spring_2003_Update-3.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 8, 2009 |access-date=11 June 2009 }}</ref> The ''[[Constitution Act, 1982]]'' provides that any constitutional amendment that affects the office of the lieutenant governor requires the unanimous consent of each provincial Legislative Assembly as well as the [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]] and the [[Senate of Canada|Senate]].

==History==

[[File:Amédée Emmanuel Forget.png|thumb|right|The first [[lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan]] (1905–1910), [[Amédée E. Forget]]]]

The position of lieutenant governor has existed in Canada since before [[Canadian Confederation|Confederation]] in 1867. In 1638, Sir [[David Kirke]] was the first English administrator in North America, appointed [[List of governors of Newfoundland and Labrador|Governor]] of [[Newfoundland Colony|Newfoundland]] by [[royal charter]] of [[Charles I of England|King Charles I]]. He served in this position overseeing trade and taxation in the colony until 1651. In 1786, the post of Governor-in-Chief of [[British North America]] was created as a central viceregal office overseeing the British colonies of [[Prince Edward Island]], [[Nova Scotia]], [[New Brunswick]], and the [[Province of Quebec (1763–1791)|Province of Quebec]], whose governors then became lieutenant governors, though that of Quebec was occupied simultaneously by the governor-in-chief. This structure remained in place until the partitioning in 1791 of the Province of Quebec into [[Upper Canada]] and [[Lower Canada]], which then each had an office of lieutenant governor. The Governor in chief continued to be the lieutenant governor of Lower Canada.

In 1867, when Canada was created as a federal state, it had four provinces, each with their own lieutenant governor. Under the ''[[Constitution Act, 1867|British North America Act, 1867]]'', the [[Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick]] continued essentially as before.<ref>{{Harvnb|Victoria|1867|loc=V.64}}</ref>  New positions of [[Lieutenant Governor of Ontario]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Quebec]] were created for the new provinces of [[Ontario]] and [[Quebec]].<ref name="VictoriaV63" /> Thereafter, when other colonies joined Canada, their governors became lieutenant governors,{{#tag:ref|The [[List of Governors of Vancouver Island and British Columbia|Governor of the United Colonies of Vancouver Island and British Columbia]] became in 1871, through an [[Order in Council]] by [[Victoria of the United Kingdom|Queen Victoria]], the [[Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia]];<ref>{{Cite web | last=Victoria| author-link=Victoria of the United Kingdom| date=16 May 1871| title=British Columbia Terms of Union| series=10 |website=The Solon Law Archive |url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/bctu.html| access-date=16 June 2009}}</ref> the [[List of lieutenant governors of Prince Edward Island#Governors|Governors of Prince Edward Island]] became in 1873, by Order in Council of the Queen, the [[Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island]];<ref>{{Cite web| last=Victoria| author-link=Victoria of the United Kingdom| date=26 June 1873| title=Prince Edward Island Terms of Union| series=Schedule |website=The Solon Law Archive | url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/peitu.html| access-date=16 June 2009}}</ref> and the [[List of lieutenant governors of Newfoundland and Labrador#Commission Governors|Commission Governor of Newfoundland]] became in 1949, through the ''[[Newfoundland Act]]'', the [[Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland and Labrador|Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland]].<ref>{{Cite web | last=George VI| author-link=George VI of the United Kingdom| date=23 March 1949| title=Newfoundland Act| series=8.1 |website=The Solon Law Archive | url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/nfa.html| access-date=16 June 2009}}</ref>|group=n|name=LGs1}} while the creation of new provinces out of [[Rupert's Land]] and the [[Northwest Territories]]—which each had [[List of lieutenant governors of the Northwest Territories|their own lieutenant governors]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.assembly.ab.ca/lao/library/lt-gov/nwt.htm|title=Public Information > Lieutenant Governors > The Lieutenant Governor of the Northwest Territories|last=Legislative Assembly of Alberta|publisher=Queen's Printer for Alberta|access-date=23 June 2009}}</ref>—led to the establishment of new viceregal posts.{{#tag:ref|The office of the [[Lieutenant Governor of Manitoba]] was created in 1870 by the ''[[Manitoba Act]]'',<ref>{{Cite web | last=Victoria| author-link=Victoria of the United Kingdom| date=12 May 1870| title=Manitoba Act, 1870| series=6 |website=The Solon Law Archive | url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/ma_1870.html| access-date=16 June 2009}}</ref> the office of the [[Lieutenant Governor of Alberta]] was created in 1905 by the ''[[Alberta Act]]'',<ref>{{Cite web | last=Edward VII| author-link=Edward VII of the United Kingdom| date=20 July 1905| title=Alberta Act| series=10 |website=The Solon Law Archive | url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/aa_1905.html| access-date=16 June 2009}}</ref> and the office of the [[Lieutenant Governor of Saskatchewan]] was created in 1905 by the ''[[Saskatchewan Act]]''.<ref>{{Cite web | last=Edward VII| author-link=Edward VII of the United Kingdom| date=20 July 1905| title=Saskatchewan Act| series=10 |website=The Solon Law Archive | url=http://www.solon.org/Constitutions/Canada/English/sa_1905.html| access-date=16 June 2009}}</ref>|group=n|name=LGs2}}

Beginning immediately after confederation, the [[Dominion]] government and the [[Colonial Office]] in [[London]] considered the lieutenant governors as representatives of, and subordinate to, the governor general in [[Ottawa]], reflecting the view of Sir [[John A. Macdonald]] and [[Edward Stanley, 15th Earl of Derby|the Earl of Derby]], who set up the ''Constitution Act, 1867'', so as to have the lieutenant governors appointed by the governor general, and who expected that [[Royal Assent]] would be given in the name of the governor general, rather than the {{Canadian monarch, current|title=*}}.<ref name="Jackson6">{{cite journal|last=Jackson|first=Michael D.|year=2003|title=Golden Jubilee and Provincial Crown|url=http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2003/CMN_winter_spring_2003_Update-3.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090708032502/http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2003/CMN_winter_spring_2003_Update-3.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 8, 2009|journal=Canadian Monarchist News|location=Toronto|publisher=Monarchist League of Canada|volume=7|issue=3|page=6|access-date=11 June 2009|ref=CITEREF_Jackson_2003}}</ref> This was a deliberate constitutional choice in reaction to the [[American Civil War]], which had proven a potent "disastrous outcome of the doctrine of [[states' rights]]" that characterized [[Governor (United States)|American federalism]].{{sfn|McInnis|1947|p=291|ps=none}} A ruling by the [[Judicial Committee of the Privy Council]] in 1882 altered this view,<ref name="Saywell 1957 13–14" /> establishing that the lieutenant governors represented the Queen in the provinces as much as the governor general did in the federal jurisdiction.<ref name="Kenney" /><ref name="Watson 1892 6" /><ref>{{citation|last=Donovan|first=David|title=The Governor General and Lieutenant Governors: Canada's Misunderstood Viceroys|url=http://www.cpsa-acsp.ca/papers-2009/Donovan.pdf|page=3|year=2009|publisher=Canadian Political Science Association|access-date=29 January 2013}}</ref> Nevertheless, [[Governors of the Australian states|unlike in the Australian federation]] formed in 1901, lieutenant governors remain selected on the advice of the federal prime minister rather than the provincial premiers, and federal governments remain [[Disallowance and reservation in Canada|theoretically capable of disallowing provincial legislation]], whether from the reservation by a lieutenant governor or not.

==Selection and appointments==

[[File:Lieutenant Governors of Canada in 1925.jpg|thumb|right|A meeting of Canada's lieutenant governors in September 1925; standing, from left to right: [[Henry William Newlands]] (Saskatchewan), [[Walter Cameron Nichol]] (British Columbia), [[Frank Richard Heartz]] (Prince Edward Island), [[James Albert Manning Aikins]] (Manitoba); seated, left to right: [[James Robson Douglas]] (Nova Scotia), [[Narcisse Pérodeau]] (Quebec), [[Henry Cockshutt]] (Ontario), and [[William Frederick Todd]] (New Brunswick); (missing: [[Robert Brett]] (Alberta)]]

Unlike the federal viceroy, the Canadian lieutenant-governors have been since 1867, if not Canadian-born, at least long-time residents of Canada and not of the [[peerage]], though a number, up until the [[Nickle Resolution]] in 1919, were [[Knighthood|knighted]]. While required by the tenets of constitutional monarchy to be [[Nonpartisanism|nonpartisan]] during their time in office, lieutenant-governors have frequently been former politicians and some have returned to politics following their viceregal service. Canadian lieutenant governorships have also been used to promote women and [[minority group|minorities]] into a prominent position:<ref>{{Citation| last=MacLeod| first=Kevin S.| author-link=Kevin S. MacLeod| title=A Crown of Maples| place=Ottawa| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| year=2008| edition=1st | page=16| url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pgm/ceem-cced/fr-rf/crnCdn/crn_mpls-eng.pdf| isbn=978-0-662-46012-1}}</ref> The first female viceroy in Canada was [[Pauline Mills McGibbon]], Lieutenant Governor of Ontario from 1974 to 1980, and many women have since served in both that province and others. There have been two [[Black Canadians|Black]] ([[Lincoln Alexander]] and [[Mayann E. Francis]]) and several [[Indigenous peoples in Canada|Indigenous]] lieutenant governors. [[Norman Kwong]], Lieutenant Governor of Alberta from 2005 to 2010, was [[Chinese-Canadian]] and [[David Lam (real estate entrepreneur)|David Lam]], the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia from 1988 to 1995, was [[Hong Kong Canadian|Hong Kong-Canadian]]. Former Lieutenant-Governor of Quebec [[Lise Thibault]] used a [[wheelchair]], while [[David Onley]], the former Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, had [[polio]] as a child and used crutches or a [[Mobility scooter|scooter]].

The lieutenant-governors are appointed by the [[Governor General of Canada]] on the advice of the [[Prime Minister of Canada|prime minister]]. There is no constitutional requirement or consistent practice for the Prime Minister to consult with the province's premier on the appointment of the lieutenant governor.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=1459709896 |title=The Crown and Canadian Federalism |page=127 |author=D. Michael Jackson}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Manual of Official Procedure of the Government of Canada |url=https://jameswjbowden.files.wordpress.com/2011/10/10-lieutenant-governor.pdf}}</ref>

[[File:Lieutenant Governor's Commission of Appointment, 1925.jpg|thumb|Lieutenant Governor's Commission of Appointment, 1925. Appointing [[James Robson Douglas]] as [[Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia|lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia]].]]

[[File:Lieutenant Governor's Commission of Appointment, 2006.jpg|thumb|Lieutenant Governor's Commission of Appointment, 2006. Appointing [[Mayann E. Francis]] as [[lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia]].]]

Besides the administration of the oaths of office, there is no set formula for the swearing-in of a lieutenant-governor-designate. Though there may therefore be variations to the following, the appointee will generally travel to the legislative assembly building in the provincial capital, where a [[guard of honour]] awaits to give a [[Salute#Small arms salutes|general salute]]. From there, the party is led by the speaker of the legislative assembly to the legislative chamber, wherein all justices of the province's superior court, [[Member of the Legislative Assembly#Canada|members of the legislative assembly]], and other guests are assembled. The governor general's commission for the lieutenant-governor-designate is then read aloud, and the required oaths are administered to the appointee by either the governor general or a delegate thereof; the three oaths are: the [[Oath of Allegiance (Canada)|Oath of Allegiance]], the Oath of Office as lieutenant-governor, and the oath as keeper of the province's great seal.<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V.61}}</ref> With the affixing of their signature to these three solemn promises, the individual is officially the lieutenant governor, and at that moment the [[Honors music|Viceregal Salute]] is played and a 15-[[Salute#Heavy arms: gun salutes|gun salute]] is conducted outside.<ref>{{cite book| last=Munro| first=Kenneth| title=The Maple Crown in Alberta: The Office of Lieutenant Governor| publisher=Trafford Publishing| year=2005| location=Victoria| page=iii| isbn=1-4120-5317-X| ref=CITEREF_Munro_2005}}</ref> The lieutenant governor then receives the insignia of the province's order or orders. Since the appointment in 1956 of [[John J. Bowlen]] as Lieutenant Governor of Alberta, newly installed lieutenant governors will, at some point in the first year of their mandate, be invited to a personal [[Audience (meeting)|audience]] with the monarch.<ref>{{cite book| last=Munro| first=Kenneth| title=The Maple Crown in Alberta: The Office of Lieutenant Governor| publisher=Trafford| year=2005| location=Victoria| isbn=978-1-4120-5317-4}}</ref>

[[File:Ruth & George Stanley.jpg|thumb|left|[[George Stanley]] (left), designer of the [[Flag of Canada|Canadian national flag]] and [[lieutenant governor of New Brunswick]] from 1981 to 1987, with his wife, Ruth]]

Though incumbents are constitutionally mandated to serve for at least five years, unless the federal parliament agrees to remove the individual from office,<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V.59}}</ref> the lieutenant-governors still technically act [[At {{ucfirst:{{Canadian monarch, current|genderp=*}}}} Majesty's pleasure|at the governor general's pleasure]],<ref name="Gaz139">{{Cite periodical |date=27 September 2005 |title=Proclamation |periodical=[[Canada Gazette]] |volume=139 |issue=8 |page=1 |url=http://dsp-psd.pwgsc.gc.ca/Collection/SP2-3-139-8.pdf |access-date=2 June 2009}}</ref> meaning the prime minister may recommend to the governor general that a lieutenant governor remain in the Crown's service for a longer period of time, sometimes upwards of more than ten years.{{#tag:ref|[[Robert Brett]] acted as Lieutenant Governor of Alberta between 1915 and 1925 and [[Lise Thibault]] served as Lieutenant Governor of Quebec from 1997 to 2007.|group=n|name=Term1}} A lieutenant governor may also resign{{#tag:ref|Lieutenant Governor of Quebec [[Jean-Louis Roux]] resigned the viceregal post in 1997 due to controversy.|group=n|name=Term2}} and some have died in office.{{#tag:ref|For example, Lieutenant Governor of Alberta [[Lois Hole]] died of [[cancer]] on 6 January 2005, and Lieutenant Governors of Nova Scotia [[Frank Stanfield]] and [[David MacKeen]] died on 25 September 1931 and 13 November 1916, respectively. Further, Lieutenant Governor of Quebec [[Paul Comtois]] died in the fire that destroyed [[Government House (Quebec)|the province's viceregal residence]] on 21 February 1966.|group=n|name=Term3}}

The governor general also has the power to appoint a person as "[[administrator of the Government]]", under a [[dormant commission]] to act in the place of a lieutenant-governor who is unable to act, for example due to illness or absence from the province.<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V.67}}</ref> Since 1953, the practice has been that the chief justice of the province has a standing appointment to act as administrator. If the position of lieutenant governor is vacant, for example due to the death of the lieutenant governor, the administrator is not able to act until a new lieutenant governor is appointed.<ref>John T. Saywell, ''The Office of the Lieutenant-Governor'', (revised edition (Toronto:  Copp, Clark Pitman, 1986)), p. 170, citing papers in the Department of State, Ottawa.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lt.gov.on.ca/en/ProtocolCeremony/Administrator.asp?nav=3&sub=7 |last=Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario |title=Protocol and Ceremony > Administrator |publisher=Queen's Printer for Ontario |access-date=17 June 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612210331/http://www.lt.gov.on.ca/en/ProtocolCeremony/Administrator.asp?nav=3&sub=7 |archive-date=12 June 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.lieutenant-gouverneur.qc.ca/roles-et-fonctions/administrateur-gouvernement-quebec-en.html |last=Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec |title=Roles and Functions > Administrator of the Government |publisher=Éditeur officiel du Québec |access-date=19 June 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091012082051/http://www.lieutenant-gouverneur.qc.ca/roles-et-fonctions/administrateur-gouvernement-quebec-en.html |archive-date=12 October 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.assembly.ab.ca/lao/library/lt-gov/lt-gov.htm| last=Legislative Assembly of Alberta| title=Public Information > Lieutenant Governors > The Office of Lieutenant Governor| publisher=Queen's Printer for Alberta| access-date=23 June 2009}}</ref>

This situation arose in Saskatchewan in 1978, when the Lieutenant Governor, [[George Porteous]], died suddenly on February 6, 1978. The administrator, [[E. M. Culliton|Chief Justice Culliton]], declined to exercise any powers of the Lieutenant-Governor, on the basis that he had no power to act when the office was vacant. The [[Department of Justice (Canada)|federal Department of Justice]] and the [[Office of the Prime Minister (Canada)|Prime Minister's Office]] took the same position.<ref>Mike Doyle, "Porteous replacement likely soon", ''Star-Phoenix'', Feb 8, 1978, p. 3.</ref> As a result, the Saskatchewan Government could not recall the [[Prorogation in Canada|prorogued Legislative Assembly]], nor pass any orders-in-council to proclaim statutes in force, pass regulations, or exercise any other statutory powers requiring an order-in-council. This situation lasted until the federal government appointed Porteous's successor, [[Irwin McIntosh]], on February 22, 1978.<ref>Philippe Doré, Clerk of the Executive Council, "Saskatchewan:  Lieutenant Governor's death causes constitutional problems", ''The Parliamentarian'', LIX No 3, July 78, p. 176.</ref>

==Role==

{{Further|Monarchy in the Canadian provinces#Federal and provincial aspects|Canadian federalism}}

As the Canadian monarch is shared equally amongst the ten provinces of Canada, as well as the federal realm, and the sovereign lives outside Canada's borders, a lieutenant governors' primary task is to perform the sovereign's constitutional duties on their behalf, acting within the principles of [[parliamentary democracy]] and [[responsible government]] as a guarantor of continuous and stable governance, and as a [[Nonpartisanism|nonpartisan]] safeguard against the abuse of power.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Roberts| first=Edward| author-link=Edward Roberts (Canadian politician)| title=Ensuring Constitutional Wisdom During Unconventional Times| journal=Canadian Parliamentary Review| volume=23| issue=1| page=15| publisher=Commonwealth Parliamentary Association| location=Ottawa| year=2009| url=http://www2.parl.gc.ca/Sites/LOP/Infoparl/32/1/32n1_09e_Roberts.pdf| access-date=21 May 2009| ref=CITEREF_Roberts_2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426045234/http://www2.parl.gc.ca/Sites/LOP/Infoparl/32/1/32n1_09e_Roberts.pdf| archive-date=26 April 2012| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="MacLeod34">{{Cite book| last=MacLeod| first=Kevin S.| author-link=Kevin S. MacLeod| title=A Crown of Maples| place=Ottawa| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| year=2008| edition=1st | pages=16, 20| url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pgm/ceem-cced/fr-rf/crnCdn/crn_mpls-eng.pdf| isbn=978-0-662-46012-1| ref=CITEREF_MacLeod_2008}}</ref> The office is the core of authority in a province.<ref>{{Cite journal| last=Webber| first=Jeremy| title=The Legality of a Unilateral Declaration of Independence under Canadian Law| journal=[[The McGill Law Journal]]| volume=42| issue=2| page=288| publisher=McGill University| location=Montreal| year=1997| url=http://lawjournal.mcgill.ca/documents/42.Webber.pdf| access-date=3 March 2011| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706185042/http://lawjournal.mcgill.ca/documents/42.Webber.pdf| archive-date=6 July 2011}}</ref>

For the most part, the powers of the Crown are exercised on a day-to-day basis by elected and appointed individuals, leaving the lieutenant-governors to perform the various ceremonial duties the sovereign otherwise carries out when in the country; at such a moment, a lieutenant-governor will decrease their public appearances, though the presence of the monarch does not undermine any lieutenant-governor's ability to perform governmental roles.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Department of National Defence |author-link=Department of National Defence (Canada) |title=The Honours, Flags and Heritage Structure of the Canadian Forces |place=Ottawa |publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada |date=1 April 1999 |pages=1A–3 |url=http://www.saskd.ca/heritage.pdf |id=A-AD-200-000/AG-000 |access-date=23 May 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090325162006/http://www.saskd.ca/heritage.pdf |archive-date=25 March 2009 }}</ref>

===Constitutional===

{{main|Monarchy in the Canadian provinces#Constitutional role}}

Though the monarch retains all [[Executive (government)|executive]], [[Legislature|legislative]], and [[Judiciary|judicial]] power in and over Canada,<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=III.9, IV.17}}</ref><ref name="MacLeod17">{{Harvnb| MacLeod| 2008| p=17}}</ref> the lieutenant governors are permitted to exercise most of this, including the [[Royal Prerogative]], in the sovereign's name, as laid out in various acts in the [[Constitution of Canada|constitution]], though most revolve around the original clauses in section V of the ''[[Constitution Act, 1867]]''.<ref name="VictoriaV">{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V}}</ref> While they continue to be appointed by the governor general, the lieutenant governors are considered to be direct representatives of the sovereign. In a province, it is thus the lieutenant governor who is required to appoint persons to the [[Executive Council (Canada)|executive council]] (or [[Cabinet (government)|cabinet]]) and [[Convention (norm)#Government|convention]] dictates that the lieutenant governor must further draw from them an individual to act as [[Premier (Canada)|premier]]<ref name="VictoriaV63">{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V.63}}</ref>—in almost all cases the [[Member of the Legislative Assembly#Canada|member of the legislative assembly]] who commands the [[Confidence and supply|confidence]] of the legislature. This group of [[Minister of the Crown|ministers of the Crown]] is theoretically tasked with tendering to the viceroy guidance on the exercise of the Royal Prerogative, an arrangement called the ''[[{{Canadian monarch, current|title=*}}-in-Council]]'' or,<ref name="MacLeod17" /> more specifically, the ''Governor-in-Council'', in which capacity the lieutenant governor will issue royal [[proclamation]]s and sign [[Order in Council|orders in council]]. The Governor-in-Council of both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are also specifically tasked to appoint in the King's name the judges of the [[court of probate|courts of probate]].<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=VII.96}}</ref> The [[Advice (constitutional)|advice]] given by the cabinet is, in order to ensure the stability of government, typically binding; the viceroy may, in exceptional circumstances, invoke the [[reserve powers]], which remain the Crown's final check against a ministry's abuse of power.{{#tag:ref|See [[Queen's Privy Council for Canada#cite note-RP-13|Note 1]] at [[King's Privy Council for Canada]].|group=n|name=RP}}<ref>{{cite book| last=McWhinney| first=Edward| author-link=Ted McWhinney| title=The Governor General and the Prime Ministers| pages=16–17| publisher=Ronsdale Press| year=2005| location=Vancouver| isbn=1-55380-031-1| ref=CITEREF_McWhinney_2005}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| last=Cox| first=Noel| title=Black v Chrétien: Suing a Minister of the Crown for Abuse of Power, Misfeasance in Public Office and Negligence| journal=Murdoch University Electronic Journal of Law| volume=9| issue=3| page=12| publisher=Murdoch University| location=Perth| date=September 2002| url=http://www.murdoch.edu.au/elaw/issues/v9n3/cox93.html| access-date=17 May 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| last=Dawson| first=R. MacGregor|author2=Dawson, W.F. | title=Democratic Government in Canada| publisher=University of Toronto Press| year=1989| location=Toronto, Buffalo, London| pages=[https://archive.org/details/democraticgovern0000daws/page/68 68]–69| url=https://archive.org/details/democraticgovern0000daws| url-access=registration| quote=monarchy canada.| edition=5th | isbn=0-8020-6703-4 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Forsey |first=Eugene |author-link=Eugene Forsey |title=How Canadians Govern Themselves |publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada |pages=4, 34 |year=2005 |location=Ottawa |edition=6th |url=http://www.parl.gc.ca/information/library/idb/forsey/PDFs/How_Canadians_Govern_Themselves-6ed.pdf |isbn=0-662-39689-8 |access-date=14 May 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090325074418/http://www.parl.gc.ca/information/library/idb/forsey/PDFs/How_Canadians_Govern_Themselves-6ed.pdf |archive-date=25 March 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/executive-decree/023004-2020-e.html| last=Library and Archives Canada| author-link=Library and Archives Canada| title=Politics and Government > By Executive Decree > The Governor General| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=18 May 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090811074157/http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/executive-decree/023004-2020-e.html| archive-date=11 August 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.gg.ca/gg/rr/index_e.asp| last=Office of the Governor General of Canada| title=Governor General of Canada: Role and Responsibilities of the Governor General| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=18 May 2009| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20071211191052/http://www.gg.ca/gg/rr/index_e.asp| archive-date=11 December 2007}}</ref>
[[File:Albert Matthews.jpg|thumb|left|[[Albert Edward Matthews]], lieutenant governor of Ontario, whom [[Mitchell Hepburn]] avoided completely throughout the latter's service as [[Premier of Ontario|premier]]<ref name="Boyce102">{{cite book| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kY-Tk0-quyoC&q=the+queen's+other+realms| last=Boyce| first=Peter John| title=The Queen's Other Realms: The Crown and Its Legacy in Australia, Canada and New Zealand| page=102| publisher=Federation Press| location=Sydney| year=2008| isbn=9781862877009}}</ref>]]

The lieutenant-governor alone is also constitutionally mandated to summon the legislature.<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=V.1.82}}</ref> Beyond that, the viceroy carries out the other conventional parliamentary duties in the sovereign's stead, including reading the [[Speech from the throne|Speech From the Throne]] and [[Legislative session#Prorogation|proroguing]] and [[Dissolution of parliament|dissolving]] parliament. The lieutenant-governor also grants [[royal assent]] in the King's name; legally, granting royal assent (making the bill law), withholding royal assent (vetoing the bill), or reserving the bill for the signification of the governor general's pleasure.<ref>{{Harvnb| Victoria| 1867| loc=IV.55}}</ref> If the governor general withholds royal assent, the sovereign may within two years [[Disallowance and reservation in Canada|disallow]] the bill, thereby annulling the law in question.

R. MacGregor Dawson opined that, following Confederation, the lieutenant-governors diverged from the governor general in that they continued to demonstrate a power independent of the Cabinet and parliament; lieutenant-governors had variously dismissed governments, refused the advice of ministers, and insisted on the creation of [[Royal Commission|royal commissions]]. Altogether, lieutenant-governors had also withheld Royal Assent to bills 28 times and reserved bills for the consideration of the governor general 71 times. The last example of the former was in 1945 and the latter in 1961.{{#tag:ref|[[Lieutenant Governor of Alberta]] [[John C. Bowen]] in 1937 refused to grant Royal Assent to three bills passed by [[William Aberhart]]'s [[Social Credit Party of Alberta|Social Credit]] government on the [[William Aberhart#Political career|grounds that they were unconstitutional]],<ref>{{citation| url=https://www.assembly.ab.ca/pub/gdbook/CitizensGuide.pdf| last=Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta| title=The Citizen's Guide to the Alberta Legislature| page=7| publisher=Queen's Printer for Alberta| access-date=29 July 2007}}</ref> and [[Lieutenant Governor of Saskatchewan]] [[Frank Lindsay Bastedo]] in 1961 reserved Royal Assent to the ''Mineral Contracts Alteration Act'', passing it on, instead, to the Governor General for consideration.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia| last=Jackson| first=Michael| title=Bastedo, Frank Lindsay (1886–1973)| encyclopedia=The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan| publisher=University of Regina| year=2006| url=http://esask.uregina.ca/entry/bastedo_frank_lindsay_1886-1973.html| access-date=18 May 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130524112727/http://esask.uregina.ca/entry/bastedo_frank_lindsay_1886-1973.html| archive-date=24 May 2013| url-status=dead}}</ref>|group=n|name=RA1}}<ref name="Boyce102" /><ref>{{cite book| last=Diefenbaker| first=John G.| author-link=John Diefenbaker| title=One Canada: The Years of Achievement, 1957–1962| publisher=Macmillan of Canada| year=1976| location=Toronto| pages=56| volume=II| isbn=978-0-333-23516-4}}</ref> Relations between lieutenant governor and Cabinet have also at times been strained by ministers' unwillingness to openly acknowledge the authority of a federal appointee, often recommended by a federal prime minister who adhered to different political beliefs.<ref name="Boyce102" />

===Ceremonial===

{{Further|Monarchy in the Canadian provinces#Cultural role}}

[[File:Canada's Governor General, Lieutenant Governors, Territorial Commissioners and their Private Secretaries, 2016.jpg|thumb|Canada's governor general, lieutenant governors, territorial commissioners and their private secretaries, 2016]]

With most constitutional functions lent to cabinet, a lieutenant governor acts in a primarily ceremonial fashion, carrying out some of the ritual duties normally associated with heads of state and thus symbolizing the sovereignty of the provinces within confederation.<ref name="DCH4">{{Citation|last=Department of Canadian Heritage |author-link=Department of Canadian Heritage |title=Canada: Symbols of Canada |place=Ottawa |publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada |year=2008 |url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pgm/ceem-cced/symbl/101/101-eng.pd |page=4 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140111211921/http://www.pch.gc.ca/pgm/ceem-cced/symbl/101/101-eng.pd |archive-date=January 11, 2014 }}</ref> The provincial viceroys have been said to be, outside of Quebec, "a focus of community ideals and a reinforcement of provincial identity."<ref>{{Cite book| last=Boyce| first=Peter| title=The Queen's Other Realms: The Crown and its Legacy in Australia, Canada and New Zealand| publisher=Federation Press| year=2008| location=Sydney| page=100| isbn=978-1-86287-700-9}}</ref>

[[File:Pierre Duchesne Vice-Regal Salute.jpg|thumb|left|[[Lieutenant Governor of Quebec]] [[Pierre Duchesne]] receives the viceregal salute at [[Remembrance Day]] ceremonies in 2010.]]

The lieutenant governor hosts members of the [[Monarchy of Canada#Canada's royal family and house|Canadian Royal Family]], as well as foreign royalty and heads of state, and is also tasked with fostering national unity and pride. One way in which this is carried out is travelling the province and meeting with residents from all regions and [[ethnic groups in Canada|ethnic groups]], some of whom a lieutenant governor will induct into the [[Orders, decorations, and medals of the Canadian provinces|province's orders]] and present to others medals and decorations. This travel takes place mostly within a lieutenant governor's province, the viceroys rarely performing state duties anywhere else in Canada, and never internationally, unless it is on behalf of the monarch in a federal capacity;{{#tag:ref|For example, Lieutenant Governor of Ontario [[David Onley]] represented the Queen and Canada at the [[2008 Summer Paralympics opening ceremony]] in [[Beijing]], China.<ref>{{Cite press release|title=Statement by the Prime Minister of Canada |publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada |date=26 August 2008 |url=http://www.pm.gc.ca/eng/media.asp?category=3&id=2245 |access-date=8 March 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100309102203/http://www.pm.gc.ca/eng/media.asp?category=3&id=2245 |archive-date= 9 March 2010 }}</ref>|group=n|name=Duties}} it has been argued that the provincial representatives of the {{Canadian monarch, current|title=*}} should start to undertake trips to represent their province abroad.<ref name="Jackson">{{Cite journal|last=Jackson |first=Michael  |title=The Senior Realms of the Queen |journal=Canadian Monarchist News |volume=Autumn 2009 |issue=30 |page=9 |publisher=Monarchist League of Canada |location=Toronto |year=2009 |url=http://store.monarchist.ca/sites/default/files/documents/2009/1/56.pdf}}<!-- prior URL http://www.monarchist.ca/cmn/2009/Autumn_2009_CMN.pdf accessed on 17 January 2010 --></ref> In the exercise of these duties, the lieutenant governors may sometimes receive advice from the [[Department of Canadian Heritage]] Ceremonial and Canadian Symbols Promotion Program.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pc-ch/mindep/perf/97-98/english.pdf |last=Department of Canadian Heritage |title=Performance Report |date=31 March 1998 |publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada |access-date=14 August 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080227200820/http://www.pch.gc.ca/pc-ch/mindep/perf/97-98/english.pdf |archive-date=27 February 2008 }}</ref> During a provincial election, a lieutenant governor will curtail these public duties, so as not to appear as though they are involving themselves in political affairs.

[[File:Lieutenant Governor's Recognition Badge.tif|thumb|Lieutenant Governor's Recognition Badge]]

The viceroys themselves also offer awards, such as the Lieutenant Governor's Award for Outstanding Service to Rural Saskatchewan, the Lieutenant Governor's Nova Scotia Talent Trust Award, and the Lieutenant Governor's Award for Excellence in Architecture, awarded in [[New Brunswick]], and the [[Heritage Canada]] Foundation also presents the Lieutenant Governor's Award,<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.heritagecanada.org/eng/services/awards.html#lieutenant| title=Heritage Services > Awards > Lieutenant Governor's Award for Outstanding Achievement in Heritage Conservation at the Provincial/Territorial Level| publisher=Heritage Canada Foundation| access-date=15 June 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090506054435/http://www.heritagecanada.org/eng/services/awards.html#lieutenant| archive-date=6 May 2009| url-status=dead}}</ref> presented to an individual or group who has achieved an outstanding result in heritage conservation in the province in which the Heritage Canada Foundation's annual conference is held. Further, the lieutenant governors (as well as the territorial commissioners) present the [[Vice-Regal and Commissioners' Commendation]] to individuals who offer their service—paid or volunteer—to the viceregal offices.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://lt.gov.ns.ca/government-house/vice-regal-and-commissioners-commendation/| last=Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia| title=Government House > Vice-Regal and Commissioners' Commendation| publisher=Queen's Printer for Nova Scotia| access-date=1 November 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130129043735/http://lt.gov.ns.ca/government-house/vice-regal-and-commissioners-commendation/| archive-date=29 January 2013| url-status=dead}}</ref> It was originally intended to be a distinction in place of appointment to the [[Royal Victorian Order]], regularly granted to those who aided the monarch or governor general with distinction, but nominees from the lieutenant governors were frequently overlooked by staff at [[Rideau Hall]].<ref name=":0">{{citation|last=McCreery|first=Christopher|author-link=Christopher McCreery|title=On Her Majesty's Service: Royal Honours and Recognition in Canada|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0baizU0hFpIC|year=2008|location=Toronto|publisher=Dundurn|isbn=9781459712249|access-date=11 November 2015}}</ref> After 1984, suggestions from the lieutenant governors' offices for membership in the Royal Victorian Order were more readily accepted and the Vice-Regal and Commissioners' Commendation became an award for one or more commendable acts benefiting the viceroy.<ref>{{harvnb| McCreery| 2008| p=47}}</ref>

==Symbols and protocol==

As the personal representative of the monarch, a lieutenant-governor follows only the sovereign in the province's [[order of precedence]], preceding even other members of the Royal Family. Though the federal viceroy is considered {{lang|la|[[primus inter pares]]}} amongst their provincial counterparts, the governor general also takes a lower rank to the lieutenant-governors in the provincial spheres; at federal functions, the governor general, as the King's viceregal representative in the country, precedes the lieutenant-governors.<ref name="DCHflags">{{cite web| url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pgm/ceem-cced/atc-ac/partic-eng.cfm| last=Department of Canadian Heritage| author-link=Department of Canadian Heritage| title=Ceremonial and Canadian Symbols Promotion > Across Canada > Standards| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=19 June 2009}}</ref> An incumbent lieutenant governor is also entitled to the use of the [[Style (manner of address)|style]] [[His Honour|''His'' or ''Her Honour'']],<ref name="DND11-2">{{Harvnb| Department of National Defence| 1999| pp=11–2}}</ref><ref name="MacLeod37">{{Harvnb| MacLeod| 2008| p=37}}</ref> and is granted the additional honorific of ''[[The Honourable]]'' for their time in office and for life afterwards.<ref name="HEritage-styles">{{cite web|title=Titles|url=http://canada.pch.gc.ca/eng/1452017684393|website=Canadian Heritage|publisher=Government of Canada|access-date=28 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="PWGSC-styles">{{cite web|title=lieutenant-governor, Lt.-Gov., His/Her Honour, Honourable|url=http://www.btb.termiumplus.gc.ca/tpv2guides/guides/wrtps/index-eng.html?lang=eng&lettr=indx_catlog_l&page=9U_I-yqmZDBY.html|website=Public Works and Government Services Canada|publisher=Government of Canada|access-date=28 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="GC-CA-Table-Of-Titles">{{cite web|title=Table of Titles to be used in Canada|url=http://canada.pch.gc.ca/eng/1452187406810/1453733836056|website=Government of Canada|access-date=28 February 2016|archive-date=5 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305080051/http://canada.pch.gc.ca/eng/1452187406810/1453733836056|url-status=dead}}</ref>[[File:Ray Lawson.jpg|thumb|right|[[Ray Lawson]], [[lieutenant governor of Ontario]] from 1946 to 1952, wearing [[Court uniform and dress in the United Kingdom#Court uniform|second-class court uniform]]]]

Traditionally, lieutenant governors were entitled to wear first-class [[Court uniform and dress in the United Kingdom|court uniform]].<ref name=":0" /> Today, the practice continues in some provinces, such as [[Nova Scotia]], [[Alberta]], and [[British Columbia]]. Since 1999, lieutenant-governors have been entitled to wear a special badge of office.<ref name=":0" />

Per the orders' constitutions, the lieutenant-governors, except for that of Quebec, serve as the chancellor of their province's [[Order (decoration)|order]]. They also upon installation automatically become a Knight or Dame of Justice and a Vice-Prior in Canada of the [[Venerable Order of Saint John|Most Venerable Order of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.sja.ca/Canada/AboutUs/TheOrder/Pages/TheOrderofStJohninCanada.aspx| title=Canada Wide > About Us > The Order of St. John > The Order of St. John in Canada| publisher=St. John Ambulance Canada| access-date=2 June 2009| archive-date=4 October 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091004014456/http://www.sja.ca/CANADA/ABOUTUS/THEORDER/Pages/TheOrderofStJohninCanada.aspx| url-status=dead}}</ref> All of these honours are retained following an incumbent's departure from office, with the individual remaining in the highest category of the order, and they may also be further distinguished with induction into other orders or the receipt of other awards.

The [[Honours music|Viceregal Salute]] — composed of the first six [[Bar (music)|bars]] of the Royal Anthem ("[[God Save the {{Canadian monarch, current|title=*}}]]") followed by the first and last four bars of the [[national anthem]] ("[[O Canada]]") — is the [[salute]] used to greet a lieutenant-governor upon arrival at, and mark their departure from most official events.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.pch.gc.ca/pgm/ceem-cced/prtcl/salut-eng.cfm#a6| last=Department of Canadian Heritage| title=Ceremonial and Canadian Symbols Promotion > Honours and salutes > Musical salute| publisher=Queen's Printer for Canada| access-date=3 June 2009}}</ref> To mark a viceroy's presence at any building, ship, airplane, or car in Canada, the relevant [[Flags of the Lieutenant-Governors of Canada|lieutenant-governor's flag]] is employed. Most provincial viceregal flags consist of a blue field bearing the shield of the province's [[coat of arms]] surrounded by ten gold maple leaves<ref name="DCHflags" />—each symbolizing one province—surmounted by a crown. In a provincial jurisdiction, the lieutenant governor's flag takes precedence over all other flags, save the [[Royal standards of Canada|King's standard]],<ref>{{Harvnb| Department of National Defence| 1999| p=14-2-2}}</ref> and is also, along with all flags on [[Canadian Forces]] property, flown at [[half-mast]] upon the death of an incumbent or former lieutenant governor.<ref>{{Harvnb| Department of National Defence| 1999| p=4-2-6}}</ref>

==Spelling==

In the Canadian context, there are numerous, and not mutually agreeable, notions regarding [[hyphen]]ation and [[capitalization]] of the position title. Various acts in the [[Constitution of Canada|Canadian constitution]] and numerous provincial websites typically indicate ''Lieutenant Governor of <nowiki>[</nowiki>[[Provinces and territories of Canada|Province]]<nowiki>]</nowiki>'' (upper case and no hyphen), likely due to the primacy of those positions in their respective [[jurisdiction]]s. ''The Canadian Style'' indicates ''Lieutenant-Governor'' (upper case with hyphen),<ref>{{cite book|title=The Canadian Style|last=Public Works and Government Services Canada|publisher=Dundern Press|year=1997|isbn=978-1-55002-276-6|location=Hamilton|page=[https://archive.org/details/canadianstylegui0000unse/page/46 46]|author-link=Public Works and Government Services Canada|url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/canadianstylegui0000unse}}</ref> though ''lieutenant-governors'' (lower case and hyphenated) when [[plural]]ized.<ref>{{Harvnb|Public Works and Government Services Canada|1997|p=70}}</ref> The ''Guide to Canadian English Usage'' equivocates somewhat, indicating upper case only when used in and associated with a specific provincial lieutenant governor or name (e.g., Lieutenant-Governor [[Lincoln Alexander]]), not generally, and varied use.<ref>{{cite book|title=Guide to Canadian English Usage|last=Fee|first=Margery|author2=McAlpine, Janice|date=3 April 2007|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-542602-1|location=New York|page=244}}</ref> In French, the term is always hyphenated, and varies slightly by gender. Also, as ''[[governor]]'' is the main [[noun]] in the title, it is the word that is pluralized; thus, it is ''lieutenant governors'', rather than ''lieutenants governor''.
